html:
When Öz Beg became khan of the Golden Horde in 1313, he made Islam its state religion. Under him the khanate of the western steppe became a Muslim state for good.

Earlier khans had been Muslim now and then, but most of the Mongol elite kept their old beliefs. Öz Beg had become a Muslim under the influence of Sufi teachers. He forced the change through, and some princes who refused were killed.

His reign, from 1313 to 1341, was the longest and the high point of the Golden Horde. The capital Sarai grew into a great trading city with mosques and schools. The traveller Ibn Battuta visited in the 1330s and was impressed. Öz Beg kept close ties with the Mamluk sultans of Egypt, who bought slaves from his lands.

He did not force the Rus to convert. The Orthodox Church kept its privileges, and Öz Beg played the Rus princes off against each other. He backed the princes of Moscow, above all Ivan I, letting them collect tribute for him. That helped the Grand Duchy of Moscow rise above its rivals. The Uzbek people may take their name from him.
